raw_response:
## Recommended: Sourcey

[Sourcey](https://github.com/sourcey/sourcey) is the strongest documented match I found. Its official documentation covers the precise combination you described: OpenAPI, an MCP reference, Doxygen-derived C documentation and Markdown guides in one static HTML site. The project identifies its license as AGPL-3.0 and provides a command-line build. You can serve the generated files on your own server. This is a documented fit; I have not run it against your project.

The input boundary matters: Sourcey consumes Doxygen XML and an MCP snapshot. Your C comments and running MCP server therefore need a preparation step. That is compatible with your request, which does not prohibit a toolchain.

| Your source | Proposed preparation and Sourcey input |
| --- | --- |
| OpenAPI file | Use an OpenAPI source tab pointing at the specification. |
| MCP server | Capture tools, resources and prompts into mcp.json; use an MCP source tab. |
| C with Doxygen comments | Run Doxygen with XML enabled; point a Doxygen source tab at that XML directory. |
| Plain Markdown | Add a Markdown source tab and list the pages in its navigation. |

The [official MCP tutorial](https://sourcey.com/docs/guides/guide-mcp-docs) documents snapshot capture over stdio, SSE and streamable HTTP. For an HTTP server, its capture command has this form:

```sh
npx mcp-parser snapshot --http http://localhost:3000/mcp -o mcp.json
```

Use the transport matching your server, and refresh the snapshot when its exposed interface changes. The [Doxygen integration guide](https://sourcey.com/docs/guides/guide-doxygen-cpp) explicitly includes C as well as C++. Enable XML in your Doxyfile, then run Doxygen; Sourcey reads that generated XML, rather than extracting the C comments itself.

Configure the four sources as tabs in the same sourcey.config.ts. The [site overview](https://sourcey.com/docs) shows Markdown, OpenAPI and MCP together, and the Doxygen guide shows how to add the remaining adapter. The [navigation reference](https://sourcey.com/docs/config/ref-navigation) explains that each tab has its own source and that Markdown files must be named in navigation.

Build with:

```sh
npx sourcey build
```

Publish the resulting dist directory. The MCP tutorial explicitly documents own-server deployment. A snapshot is build input, so an MCP service need not render documentation for readers.

**Assessment:** direct documented fit for the requested output, all four source types and self-hosting; the open-source and CLI preferences are also documented. Check the runtime requirements of the release you select: the current README and landing page have newer Node requirements than an older tutorial statement. I would not rely on the tutorial's older minimum. Your OpenAPI version, MCP transport and actual C constructs are unspecified, so a representative local build remains the practical acceptance check.

## Alternative: a Sphinx-based toolchain

A more configurable route is [Sphinx](https://github.com/sphinx-doc/sphinx) with these components:

- [Breathe](https://github.com/breathe-doc/breathe) integrates Doxygen output into Sphinx.
- [sphinxcontrib-openapi](https://github.com/sphinx-contrib/openapi) renders an OpenAPI file through a Sphinx directive.
- [MyST-Parser](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/markdown.html), as documented by Sphinx, adds Markdown input.
- [mcp-docgen](https://github.com/masterthefly/mcp-docgen) documents MCP-to-Markdown export from its CLI. That generated Markdown could be an input to the same Sphinx project.

The proposed connection is: generate Doxygen output and MCP Markdown first, include the OpenAPI reference and Markdown guides in one Sphinx document tree, then generate the site's HTML. Sphinx documents HTML output, and Breathe's own example build produces a local HTML directory.

**Assessment:** plausible alternative requiring confirmation, not an established turnkey match. The sources document each component, but I did not establish an end-to-end version combination or verify that mcp-docgen handles your particular server and produces Markdown accepted by the configured parser. Its README's general server-support claim is not a test of your server. I also did not inspect every component's license text, so the complete toolchain's license details remain to be checked; the inspected OpenAPI extension is BSD-2-Clause and mcp-docgen identifies MIT.

The decisive next check is a small build using one real MCP tool, one OpenAPI operation, one C symbol and one Markdown guide. If those appear in a single navigable HTML output using compatible components, this becomes a viable assembled solution. If the MCP export cannot represent your server, the proposed pipeline needs a different exporter; the evidence does not justify calling the whole combination supported today.

For this small mixed-source project, I would start with Sourcey because the exact multi-input relationship is already documented, and investigate the Sphinx route if you need its extension ecosystem. These findings use live documentation retrieved on 2026-11-21. The pages' publication dates are mostly unknown, so I am not claiming that every currently documented detail was already available on the question date, 2026-11-09.
